paper_title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Language models are increasingly deployed as agents that act in an environment over many steps to reach goal, with the model running inside harness that gives it tools, executes its actions and manages the history it sees (Yao et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). coding agent, for example, explores repository and runs shell commands, while personal assistant calls the APIs of everyday applications on behalf of user (Trivedi et al., 2024). In both cases the quality of the agent rests on its policy, that is, on the action it chooses given the task and everything that has happened so far. Obtaining such policy is post-training problem, and the usual way to solve it is reinforcement learning in the environment (Kimi Team et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025). An alternative, especially for smaller models, is to distill the policy from stronger teacher model that is already capable on long-horizon agentic tasks, by supervised fine-tuning on its trajectories (Pan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). The standard recipe supervises the full trajectory, which typically consists of chain-ofthought (CoT), some visible commentary and an action such as shell command or an API call. We study this setting for students that are already post-trained reasoning models, which reason well on single-turn problems but remain weak on long-horizon tasks. Distilling new policy into such model has to add capability without losing the ones it already has, making it continual-learning problem. Training on the teachers CoT then has practical limit. The strongest teachers are closed models behind an API whose reasoning is hidden, since providers such as OpenAI return encrypted reasoning items and at most summary, and they encrypt the reasoning precisely to prevent this kind of distillation (Panfilov et al., 2026). The teachers reasoning may also not suit the student, since small models have been found to learn poorly from traces of strong reasoners (Li et al., 2025). 1 Preprint. In this paper we show that the CoT can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teachers actions alone. To this end, we render each teacher turn into training target in which the reasoning block is left empty and is followed directly by the action. To limit drift from the initial model, we regularize the student toward its initial checkpoint with replay buffer, as is common in the continual-learning literature and in KL-regularized fine-tuning (Li & Hoiem, 2017; Rolnick et al., 2019; Ziegler et al., 2020). Concretely, every batch also contains few of the students own generations on prompts from another domain, and KL term computed on them pulls the student toward its initial checkpoint. The student is then evaluated with its thinking enabled. As result, no reasoning is ever supervised, yet at inference the student still reasons in its own way while its high-level behaviour follows the teachers policy, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Such transfer across formats has been observed before, in safety setting. Fine-tuning reasoning model with its CoT disabled on narrowly misaligned data produces broad misalignment that persists once the CoT is re-enabled at evaluation (Chua et al., 2025). We ask whether the same mechanism can transfer useful policy. One reason to expect so is that failures of language models on long tasks have been attributed to execution rather than to reasoning (Sinha et al., 2026). If execution is what fails, then the actions may be all that needs to be taught, and the students own reasoning, which is already good on single turns, can be left as it is. The teachers reasoning is nevertheless useful, and we show that the student can still benefit from it without training on the CoT directly. For this purpose we give the student proxy for the teachers reasoning, which we call CoT-proxy: short summary of that reasoning, placed after the empty reasoning block, that serves as an additional training target explaining the action that follows. The aim is to pass the student signal about what the teacher was thinking without making it imitate the CoT itself, and we show that this simple substitution works. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies require access to the full hidden CoT, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers, whose APIs return only reasoning summaries. We show that such distillation is possible in practice. Our contributions are as follows. We propose recipe that distills teachers long-horizon policy into post-trained reasoning student from the teachers actions alone, with an empty reasoning block in every training target and KL replay term that holds the student near its initial model. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified the policy transfers to 4B and 32B student, which then execute it with their own reasoning at inference. We propose CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teachers reasoning that give the student signal about the teachers CoT without having it imitate the CoT itself. Added to actiononly training, they improve task success in every setting. We show that action-only and CoT-proxy training apply to closed teachers, whose CoT is hidden behind an API, and demonstrate it on GPT-5.6 Luna, using only its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns. We test which parts of the recipe matter, finding that the replay data has to come from outside the target environment and that the summary has to sit outside the think block, and investigate how each training target changes the students reasoning at inference.

sections.title: 2 METHOD
sections.content: This section describes how we turn teacher trajectories into training targets, how CoT-proxies provide signal about the teachers reasoning without reproducing it, and how we limit drift from the initial model while it learns new policy. Problem setting. An agent trajectory is sequence of turns. In each turn the model produces hidden reasoning inside think block, opened by the token <think> and closed by </think>, then optionally some visible prose, and finally an action, which can be Python cell or bash command that the harness executes. The harness returns an observation and the next turn begins. We refer to the mapping from the task and the history of previous actions and observations to the next action as the policy. We refer to the models performance with thinking enabled on single-turn reasoning benchmarks as its single-turn capability. 2 Preprint.

Each teacher turn is rendered into target with prefilled prefix (grey, no loss) and supervised remainder (blue). The full-CoT target prefills only the opening of the reasoning block and supervises the teachers thought and action; the action-only target prefills an empty block and supervises only the action; the CoT-proxy target additionally supervises summary of the thought between the empty think block and the action. At inference only the opening token is prefilled, allowing the student to generate its own reasoning before acting (green). The inference row illustrates the intended structure, not constraint enforced on generated responses. Earlier turns of trajectory are rendered in the same representation as the target turn. Distilling the policy from actions. Each teacher turn is rendered into one of three training targets, illustrated in Figure 1. The full-CoT target is the conventional one, in which the think block holds the teachers reasoning and everything after the opening token is supervised, the reasoning as well as the closing token and the action. The action-only target instead prefills an empty think block and supervises only the action that follows it. The empty block receives no loss, so it conditions the supervised tokens without teaching the student to produce an empty block itself. The chosen representation is applied to every turn of trajectory, including the earlier assistant turns that form the context of later one, so that an action-only example never exposes the teachers reasoning through its history. At inference every student, whatever its training target, generates with its thinking enabled. Only the opening token is prefilled, the student fills the think block with its own reasoning, and that reasoning is kept in the history of later turns. We call the transfer of policy learned from targets without reasoning to this inference setting cross-format transfer. CoT-proxies. The CoT-proxy target puts part of the teachers reasoning back, but outside the think block and in condensed form. It keeps the empty think block of the action-only target and inserts short summary of the teachers reasoning, wrapped in <summary> block, between the empty block and the action. The summary is meant to capture the decision behind the action rather than the reasoning itself, and it never enters the think block. For the open teacher we obtain the summaries offline by asking the teacher to condense each turns own reasoning into at most two sentences, given only that turns thought and neither the action nor later observations. For the closed teacher, in our case an OpenAI model, we use the reasoning summaries that its API returns alongside the visible output, without any further processing. Appendix describes the full summarization pipeline, including the prompts. Replay regularization. To limit changes to the students existing capabilities, we regularize it toward its initial checkpoint on fixed replay corpus. Before fine-tuning, the initial student generates responses to pool of prompts from outside the target environment, so that the regularization anchors the student to its general behaviour rather than to the task being distilled, and every training update then mixes small number of these replay samples with the teacher samples. Teacher samples receive cross-entropy supervision on their target, while replay samples receive KL penalty that pulls the trained students next-token distribution toward that of the initial student on the same saved responses. related approach recovers capability lost to fine-tuning by on-policy distillation from the initial model (Lu & Thinking Machines Lab, 2025); our penalty instead uses fixed corpus of the initial models generations and needs no sampling during training. 3 Preprint. sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Environments. We study policy distillation in two long-horizon environments. AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) asks an agent to operate everyday applications through their APIs on behalf of user, and we use its test-normal split of 168 tasks grouped into 56 scenarios, reporting task goal completion (TGC), which we also call task success, and scenario goal completion (SGC), which requires every task of scenario to succeed. SWE-bench Verified (Jimenez et al., 2024) asks an agent to resolve GitHub issue in repository through shell commands, and we report the resolved rate over its 500 tasks. Our AppWorld harness follows the ReAct setup of the AppWorld release, with the one-shot demonstration from LOOP (Chen et al., 2025), and our SWE harness is adapted from mini-swe-agent (Yang et al., 2024). Every model, whether teacher, initial student or trained student, is evaluated in the same harness with the same prompts, budgets and grader, so that the models we compare differ only in how they were trained. Students and teachers. The students are Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, referred to as Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025), both post-trained reasoning models that reason in think block by default. The open teacher is Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) and the closed teacher is GPT5.6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026), queried at reasoning effort xhigh through the Responses API with its encrypted reasoning items carried across turns. Teacher data. Teacher data comes from rolling out each teacher on training tasks that are disjoint from the evaluation tasks. On AppWorld these are the 90 tasks of the official training split, and each teacher is run three times on each of them, which gives 270 trajectories per teacher, with 3,704 turns for the open teacher and 4,218 for the closed one. sections.title: 4 RESULTS
sections.content: Tables 1 and 2 contain the main results for the open and the closed teacher. In every table number is the mean over three seeds, followed by its standard deviation. Appendix D.4 tests the differences between targets with paired statistics over tasks and seeds. Actions alone transfer the policy. The action-only configuration in Table 1 shows that policy can be learned from targets that contain no reasoning at all. On AppWorld, task success for Qwen34B increases from 7.3% to 17.9% and for Qwen3-32B from 11.5% to 25.4%. On SWE-bench it increases from 2.7% to 5.5% for Qwen3-4B and from 5.8% to 14.3% for Qwen3-32B. In every one of these evaluations the student fills its think block before it acts, so the learned policy is carried out by the students own reasoning. Full-CoT training, which keeps the teachers reasoning in the target, is ahead of action-only training in two of the four settings, by 11 points for the 4B student on AppWorld and by 7 points for the 32B student on SWE-bench. In the other two settings the two targets are within three points of each other. Dropping the teachers reasoning therefore costs task success in some settings but not in others, and the next paragraph shows that CoT-proxies recover this loss. The full-CoT student also takes the most turns per task of the trained students in every setting, yet it is the best in none of them, so the additional steps do not turn into success. On AppWorld it is also the student that most often exhausts its token budget, in 20% of the trajectories for Qwen3-4B and 35% for Qwen3-32B against at most 10% for the other trained students, which suggests that it struggles to bring its tasks to an end. Ending within the budget does not imply success, however: the initial models end within the budget in 8099% of the trajectories and yet solve the fewest tasks. CoT-proxies add to what actions alone teach. Adding summary of the teachers reasoning after the empty think block raises Qwen3-4B from 17.9% to 34.5% on AppWorld and from 5.5% to 15.1% on SWE-bench. The CoT-proxy students have the highest mean in every column of Table 1, although their lead over full-CoT training is statistically significant only for Qwen3-4B on SWEbench. The signal costs no reasoning tokens, since the student still never trains on the teachers reasoning, and the summaries are far shorter than the reasoning they condense, on average 26 tokens against 124 on AppWorld and 20 against 81 on SWE-bench. The recipe transfers to closed teacher. Table 2 repeats the AppWorld experiment with GPT-5.6 Luna as the teacher, stronger model that solves 89.3% of the test tasks against 60.7% for the open teacher. Its reasoning is hidden, and its API returns summary of that reasoning together with the visible response. The action-only target is therefore built from the visible responses alone, and the CoT-proxy target places the API summary between the empty think block and the action, in the same position as the summaries we generate for the open teacher. Action-only training again transfers the policy, raising task success from 7.3% to 35.1% for Qwen3-4B and from 11.5% to 44.4% for Qwen332B, and CoT-proxy training raises it further, to 48.2% and 59.1%, respectively. sections.title: 5 ABLATIONS
sections.content: Beyond the targets themselves, the recipe rests on four choices: the replay regularization, the placement of the summary outside the think block, the source of the summary, and the removal of the teachers visible text. This section tests each of them with additional training runs of the 4B student on AppWorld, keeping everything else in the recipe fixed. Replay fraction. Table 3 trains each target with and without replay regularization. Without replay, full-CoT training lowers AIME accuracy from 74.7% to 68.9% and raises the held-out KL divergence from the initial model from 0.003 to 0.042 nats per token. The action-only and CoTproxy targets lose less on AIME without replay, while their divergence rises in the same way, and replay removes that rise as well. On IFEval and MMLU-Pro every configuration stays within about one point of the initial model, and the regularized run is ahead in each pair as well. Replay also brings small gain in task success. On AppWorld it rises from 28.2% to 29.2% for fullCoT, from 14.3% to 17.9% for action-only and from 29.4% to 34.5% for CoT-proxy. The regularized run is ahead in every pair, although the differences lie within the seed spread. Replay domain. Table 4 replaces the out-of-domain replay pool with an in-domain one, built by running the initial student three times on each of the 90 AppWorld training tasks and sampling 1,000 of its responses, each kept with the context it was generated in. Task success drops for the three targets, and the action-only student ends at the 7.3% of the initial model. Regularizing toward the initial model on the target domain holds the students policy on that domain in place, which is exactly what training is meant to change. The replay data therefore has to come from outside the target environment. Summary placement. Table 5 tests whether the CoT-proxy gain depends on where the summary is placed. For this we train summary-as-CoT variant on the same teacher trajectories and summaries as the CoT-proxy target, but instead of placing each turns summary after an empty think block, we place it inside the think block, where the full-CoT target has the teachers reasoning. The student is then trained on these targets exactly as on full-CoT targets, with only the opening token prefilled and the summary, the closing token and the action supervised, so the summary serves as short chain-of-thought. With the open teachers summaries this variant reaches 23.4% against 34.5% for CoT-proxies, and with the closed teachers summaries 33.9% against 48.2%. It also falls below full-CoT training, at 29.2% for the open teacher. summary is therefore poor substitute for the teachers reasoning inside the think block, but useful signal outside it as CoT-proxy. Summary source. The summaries of the open teacher are written by the teacher model itself with thinking enabled, and almost all of the generation cost is the annotators own reasoning (Appendix A). sections.title: 7 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Reinforcement learning is the main route to long-horizon agents. Kimi Team et al. (2026) combine large-scale agentic data synthesis pipeline with joint reinforcement learning stage, Cao et al. (2026) synthesize verifiable coding tasks with executable environments and learn from their feedback, Luo et al. (2025) train Qwen3-32B on software engineering tasks with reinforcement learning alone, and Chen et al. (2025) train an agent on AppWorld with leave-one-out variant of PPO. When stronger teacher exists, supervised fine-tuning on its trajectories is the cheaper alternative, and much of the work on open agents goes into collecting such trajectories at scale. Pan et al. (2025) sample them from strong models in SWE-Gym, Ludwig et al. (2026) fine-tune in two stages on trajectories of Qwen3-Coder-480B, and Pi et al. (2026) release most of their terminal trajectory corpus together with the models trained on it. We take the supervised route, fine-tuning post-trained reasoning student to extend its capabilities to long-horizon tasks, but where this fine-tuning normally includes the teachers CoT, we show that the actions alone are enough to transfer the policy, which opens the same route to closed teachers. For closed teachers, whose APIs return at most summary of the reasoning and encrypt the rest to prevent distillation, Penaloza et al. (2026) conclude that hidden reasoning breaks standard distillation and propose two alternatives: training teacher conditioned on privileged information jointly with an unconditioned student within the same model, and on-policy self-distillation, which trains the student with reinforcement learning and reverse-KL penalty toward that teacher. We reach the same data condition with supervised fine-tuning alone, and show that the reasoning summaries an API returns suffice as an additional signal. Cross-format transfer, where reasoning model is trained with its CoT disabled and the effect of training persists at inference with the CoT enabled, has so far appeared as safety result. Betley et al. (2025) find that fine-tuning model only on writing insecure code makes it broadly misaligned, and Chua et al. (2025) show that the same happens when reasoning model is fine-tuned on such narrow behavior with its CoT disabled and evaluated with the CoT re-enabled. We use this transfer deliberately, to teach useful long-horizon policy, and measure where it lands and what it costs the students own reasoning.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We have shown that teachers long-horizon policy can be distilled into post-trained reasoning student without training on the teachers CoT. The student learns from targets whose reasoning block is empty, thinks at inference, and is held near its initial model by KL penalty on replay buffer of its own generations. CoT-proxies add signal about the teachers reasoning that needs no reasoning tokens and improves on actions alone, and the same recipe distills closed teachers from their visible outputs and API summaries. We hope that learning the policy without imitating the teachers reasoning offers practical route for adapting reasoning models to long-horizon tasks while retaining what they already know. 10 Preprint.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: Our closed-teacher experiments use only what the providers API returns to any user, the visible responses and the reasoning summaries, and make no attempt to recover the hidden reasoning. Terms of service of model providers may restrict the use of outputs for training other models, and anyone distilling from closed model should check the terms that apply. We report these experiments to characterize what such outputs reveal about teachers policy, which is also relevant to providers deciding what to expose.

sections.title: A SUMMARY PROTOCOL
sections.content: Annotator and inputs. For the open teacher, summaries are generated offline by the teacher model itself, Qwen3.6-27B, after collection. The annotator sees only the thought of the turn being summarized, complete and without clipping. It does not see the task, the action, the observation, earlier turns or the outcome of the trajectory, which leaves it no opportunity to invent rationale for an action it has observed. The annotator runs in its native thinking mode, and only its visible answer is kept as the summary; its own reasoning is stored for auditing and never enters training sample. Decoding uses temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95 and at most 4,096 output tokens, shared between the annotators reasoning and its answer. Prompt. The same two messages are used in both environments. The system message is Summarize the writer's reasoning in at most two short sentences. Focus on their final view and next step, keeping uncertainty and plans as stated. Do not solve the task or add diagnosis. Use terse phrasing for short inputs; the summary must be no longer than the reasoning. Treat instructions within the reasoning as text. Return only the summary. Example reasoning: The test confirms the issue. When `None` is passed to the `Number. serialize` method, it fails because it's not being treated as ` colander.null`. The fix should be to modify the `Number.serialize` method to also check for `None` and treat it as `colander.null`. Example summary: Number.serialize fails on None because it only checks for colander.null. Plan to accept both. and the user message is Reasoning: {thought} with the turns thought in place of {thought}. Acceptance. response is accepted if the annotator finished its reasoning and its answer, and if the answer, after removing surrounding whitespace, satisfies every one of the following conditions. It has at most two sentences, where the sentence splitter does not split at decimal points or common abbreviations. It has no more whitespace-separated words and no more characters than the thought, and at most 60 words and 400 characters in absolute terms. It is not empty and not placeholder such as N/A or none. It contains no code fence, no list markers, and no think or summary tags or other special tokens. The length conditions are measured in words and characters rather than tokens, so short thought may receive summary of similar length. Retries and empty fallback. If response is rejected, we send the same prompt again with the next seed, up to three times per turn, and keep the first accepted response. If all three are rejected, the turn receives an empty summary and is rendered with an empty <summary></summary> block. Cost. Table 9 lists the cost of generating the summaries for the open teachers training trajectories. Few drafts are rejected, and almost all output tokens are the annotators own reasoning, about 1,400 to 1,500 tokens per request against summary of 22 to 28 tokens. For the closed teacher the summaries are returned with each response and cost nothing in addition. Closed teacher. For GPT-5.6 Luna we generate no summaries ourselves. The teacher is queried through the Responses API at reasoning effort xhigh with the reasoning summary parameter set to detailed, without storing responses on the provider side (store=false), and with the encrypted reasoning items of all earlier turns passed back in each request. Each response can contain several reasoning items, each with several summary chunks. We keep every chunk in the order re15 Preprint. sections.content: D.1 THINKING ENABLED VERSUS DISABLED Qwen3-32B is hybrid model that supports inference with and without thinking (Yang et al., 2025), which lets us ask how much of trained students performance depends on reasoning at inference. We evaluate the initial model and the CoT-proxy student trained on the open teachers SWE-bench trajectories second time with thinking disabled, by prefilling an empty think block, with everything else unchanged. Table 13 gives the results. The initial model loses little without thinking, whereas the CoT-proxy student drops from 21.7% to 5.1%, so its gain rests on reasoning at inference. Without thinking, both also take more turns per task. D.2 CONTENT OF THE SUMMARY To test whether CoT-proxy students use what the summaries say, we train further Qwen3-4B students on the open teachers AppWorld and SWE-bench trajectories with the CoT-proxy recipe, with the summaries randomly permuted across all turns of all training trajectories, so that each turn carries well-formed summary written for another step. All other training text, the retained turns and the loss masks are identical to CoT-proxy. Table 14 shows that the shuffled-summary students do not come close to CoT-proxy: they are 5 points above action-only on AppWorld and below it on SWEbench. The gain of CoT-proxy therefore comes from the content of the summaries rather than from the presence of summary block. 19 Preprint.
